  Learn how to query genomic datasets, apply metadata filters, perform structured

```{r, include = FALSE}
seqout::SeqoutDefault(NULL)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

Four functions search the index:

*   `SeqoutSearch()`: Finds studies that match a text query or filters.
*   `SampleSearch()`: Finds individual samples for a cohort.
*   `Paper()`: Finds the datasets that are linked to a publication.
*   `Author()`: Finds the datasets that are linked to a researcher.

All four functions use the REST API.

```{r setup}
library(seqout)
```

## Search for studies

`SeqoutSearch()` finds matches in the study titles, abstracts, and experimental designs of all archives.

```{r first-search}
SeqoutSearch("liver cancer scRNA", limit = 5)
```

The `source` column shows the archive that holds each study.

A query with an incorrect word still runs. `SearchSuggest()` shows the
correction that the server applies to the query. `SearchFacets()` counts the
matches for each organism, platform, country and other fields. It gets no rows,
so you can know the size of a query before you run it:

```{r suggest-facets}
SearchSuggest("hepatocelular carcinoma")

f <- SearchFacets("hepatocellular carcinoma")
attr(f, "total")
head(f[f$facet == "organism", ], 5)
```

### Apply search filters

Filters decrease the number of results. You can use filters without query text.

```{r filters-only}
SeqoutSearch(organism = "Mus musculus", assay_l1 = "Transcriptomic", limit = 5)
```

Use a query together with filters:

```{r filters}
SeqoutSearch(
  "liver",
  organism         = "Homo sapiens",
  library_strategy = "RNA-Seq",
  limit            = 5
)
```

### Supported search filters

| Filter | Selection Criteria |
| --- | --- |
| `db` or `source` | One archive (for example, `geo` or `sra`). |
| `organism` | Scientific name of the target organism. |
| `library_strategy`, `library_source`, `platform`, `instrument_model` | Library preparation and sequencing. |
| `assay_l1`, `assay_l2` | Assay category and specific protocol. |
| `country`, `geo_country_code_iso2`, `geo_lat`, `geo_lng`, `geo_radius_km` | Geographic origin of the study. |
| `journal` | Journal of the linked publication. |
| `multi_platform` | Mapped studies that use more than one sequencing platform. |
| `date_from`, `date_to` | Range of the last modification date (`yyyy-mm-dd`). |

> [!WARNING]
> You cannot use `library_source` together with `assay_l1`, `assay_l2` or a `geo_*` filter. The search indexes of these filters do not work together.

When you use `db` or `source`, you must also give one or more other search terms or filters:

```{r one-archive}
SeqoutSearch("hepatocellular carcinoma", db = "geo", limit = 5)
```

`assay_l1` is a general category (`"Transcriptomic"`). `assay_l2` is a protocol (`"ATAC-seq"`):

```{r assay}
SeqoutSearch("liver", assay_l2 = "ATAC-seq", limit = 5)
```

### Browse filter vocabularies

Filter values must be the same as the values on the server. Each vocabulary has a `List*()`
function that shows the permitted values.

`ListOrganisms()` returns all the organisms in the index, more than 300,000 names. Filter the result. Do not print all of it:

```{r organisms, eval = FALSE}
organisms <- ListOrganisms()
organisms[grepl("^Mus ", organisms$scientific_name), ]
```

```{r vocabularies}
ListLibraryStrategies()
head(ListInstrumentModels())
ListPlatforms()[, c("platform", "display_name", "total")]
head(ListAssays())
ListCenters(limit = 5)
ListJournals(limit = 5)
```

These functions change country names to ISO 3166-1 alpha-3 codes, and codes to names. They work offline:

```{r countries}
CountryCodeToName(c("IND", "USA"))
CountryNameToCode("India")
```

### Filter by date

```{r dates}
SeqoutSearch("liver cancer",
  date_from = "2024-01-01", date_to = "2024-01-31", limit = 5
)
```

```{r dates-combined}
nrow(SeqoutSearch("liver", assay_l1 = "Transcriptomic", date_from = "2025-01-01"))
```

## Structured boolean searches

A structured query can use these operators:

*   Parentheses `()` put terms in a group.
*   Double quotes `""` find an exact phrase.
*   A `*` finds a prefix.
*   The uppercase operators `AND`, `OR` and `NOT` join terms.

```{r boolean}
SeqoutSearch('("aging" OR "aged") (gut OR colon) immun*', limit = 5)
```

An implicit `AND` joins adjacent terms. A boolean query finds only the exact terms. It does not add synonyms, and it does not correct words. `structured = TRUE` gives the same result for a query that has no boolean operators:

```{r boolean-forced}
SeqoutSearch("liver cancer", limit = 3)$accession
SeqoutSearch("liver cancer", structured = TRUE, limit = 3)$accession
```

> [!CAUTION]
> Only the full-text search fields parse boolean operators. If you use a boolean query with filters like `assay_l1`, `assay_l2`, or `geo_*`, the function raises an error.

```{r boolean-clash, error = TRUE}
SeqoutSearch("liver NOT mouse", assay_l1 = "Transcriptomic")
```

## Control term expansion

The server adds synonyms to each query term. The synonyms come from eight ontologies:
`MONDO`, `MeSH`, `HGNC`, `CHEBI`, `UBERON`, `CL`, `EFO` and `CVCL`. A search for
`"masld"` also finds "nafld".

`expand = FALSE` searches for the words as you typed them. `structured = TRUE`
sends the same request:

```{r expand-off}
nrow(SeqoutSearch("spinal muscular atrophy"))
nrow(SeqoutSearch("spinal muscular atrophy", expand = FALSE))
```

To remove the synonyms of one ontology and keep the others, put its name in `exclude_ontology`:

```{r exclude-ontology}
nrow(SeqoutSearch("spinal muscular atrophy", exclude_ontology = c("MeSH", "CVCL")))
```

If two ontologies supply a synonym, the synonym stays while one of the two
ontologies is on. The graph holds one node for each name. That node has the
identifiers of all the ontologies that supply the name. A name that is not one
of the eight ontologies raises an error, because the server ignores a name that
it does not know.

## Case-sensitive search

The search ignores case, so `"LINE"` also finds all instances of "cell line".
Set `case_sensitive = TRUE` to make the search obey case. Each query word must
then be a whole word in the title or summary, in the case that you typed:

```{r case-sensitive}
nrow(SeqoutSearch("LINE", limit = 1000))
nrow(SeqoutSearch("LINE", case_sensitive = TRUE, limit = 1000))
```

The words still obey the `OR`, `AND` and `NOT` operators of the query. A `*` at
the end of a word still finds a prefix. The search does not correct words.
Filters such as `assay_l1` and `geo_*` have no case-sensitive match. If you use
one of these filters with `case_sensitive`, an error occurs.

## Explore ontology mappings

`Ontology()` returns a query term, its synonyms and its child terms in the graph:

```{r ontology}
onto <- Ontology("liver")
onto
```

The `xrefs` column holds the ontology CURIEs of each row (UBERON, MeSH, MONDO, HGNC and others):

```{r ontology-xrefs}
onto$xrefs[[1]]
```

If `has_children` is set for a child, that child has its own sub-terms:

```{r ontology-children}
kids <- onto[onto$relation == "child" & onto$has_children, "name"]
head(kids, 5)
```

The server returns a maximum of 500 synonyms and 300 children. The attributes show the totals and if the server truncated the list:

```{r ontology-attrs}
attr(onto, "synonym_total")
attr(onto, "children_truncated")
```

`max_hops` (1 to 4, default 2) sets the depth of the synonym walk. `children = FALSE` does not get child terms. This call is less expensive when you want only identifiers:

```{r ontology-cheap}
Ontology("breast cancer", children = FALSE)$xrefs[[1]]
```

If the graph does not have a term, the function returns an empty data frame:

```{r ontology-missing}
nrow(Ontology("not a real term at all"))
```

### Map a metadata column to identifiers

A metadata table holds free text, for example "T cell", "hepatocyte" and "HeLa".
`MapToOntology()` finds each label in the same graph. It puts the identifiers
in a `<column>_ontology_id` column next to the label:

```{r map-to-ontology}
meta <- data.frame(celltype = c("T cell", "hepatocyte", "HeLa"))
MapToOntology(meta, "celltype")
```

`ontology` keeps the identifiers from one source. To map more than one column, give more than one column name:

```{r map-to-ontology-cl}
MapToOntology(meta, "celltype", ontology = "CL")
```

If the graph does not have a label, the result is `NA`. The function reads only
the identifiers of the label. If a label has no identifiers, `use_synonyms = TRUE` lets it use the identifiers of its synonyms:

```{r map-to-ontology-synonyms}
MapToOntology(data.frame(celltype = "nbc"), "celltype", use_synonyms = TRUE)
```

Synonym links can connect a label to narrower concepts. Each different label uses one request.

## Sort results and manage limits

The server sorts results by relevance. `sortby` (`"citations"`, `"journal"` or `"year"`) and `order` (`"desc"` or `"asc"`) change the sort order:

```{r sortby}
SeqoutSearch("hepatocellular carcinoma", sortby = "citations", limit = 5)
```

### Retrieve total match counts

The server returns results in pages of 200 rows. The `total` attribute holds the number of matches. The `took_ms` attribute holds the server time:

```{r all-rows}
result <- SeqoutSearch("hepatocellular carcinoma scRNA")
nrow(result)
attr(result, "took_ms")
```

`limit` sets the maximum number of rows. It also sets the number of pages that the function downloads:

```{r limit}
nrow(SeqoutSearch("hepatocellular carcinoma scRNA", limit = 50))
```

## Query datasets from search results

`SeqoutGet()` returns all the metadata of a study:

```{r dataset}
top <- SeqoutSearch("hepatocellular carcinoma", sortby = "citations", limit = 1)
d <- SeqoutGet(top$accession[1])

d$meta$title
c(samples = nrow(d$samples), runs = nrow(d$runs))
```

For more information, refer to [Metadata](metadata.html).

## Find datasets by publication and author

`Paper()` uses a PubMed ID (`pmid`) or a DOI (`doi`) to find the datasets that are linked to a paper:

```{r paper-pmid}
Paper(pmid = "34764296")
```

The `via` column shows if the archive deposit declared the link or if `seqout` found it.

```{r paper-doi}
Paper(doi = "10.1038/s41467-021-26864-x")
```

If no datasets are linked to a paper, the function returns an empty data frame:

```{r paper-unknown}
nrow(Paper(pmid = "999999999"))
```

`Author()` uses the full name of a researcher to find the datasets of that researcher:

```{r author}
regev <- Author("Aviv Regev")

nrow(regev)
head(regev[, c("accession", "title", "journal", "citation_count")], 5)
```

The name must be the same as the name in the publication record. Initials (`"Regev A"`) do not match:

```{r author-initials}
nrow(Author("Regev A"))
```

`limit` sets the maximum number of records that the function returns (default 200):

```{r author-limit}
nrow(Author("Aviv Regev", limit = 5))
```

## Corpus-wide collections

Each collection has three functions:

*   `*_summary()` gives the corpus totals.
*   `*_facets()` gives the filter values.
*   `*_projects()` gives the studies. With `limit = NULL`, it reads all the pages.

```{r collections}
# single-cell studies with genetic or chemical perturbation evidence
PerturbationSummary()
pf <- PerturbationFacets()
pf[pf$facet == "perturbation_type", ]
PerturbationProjects(min_confidence = "medium", data_availability = "both", limit = 10)

# spatial transcriptomics studies, by named platform
SpatialSummary()
sf <- SpatialFacets()
head(sf[sf$facet == "platform", ])
SpatialProjects(platform = "Xenium", organism = "Homo sapiens", limit = 10)

# single-cell corpus, any archive
SingleCellSummary()
scf <- SingleCellFacets()
head(scf[scf$facet == "chemistry", ])
SingleCellProjects(chemistry = "10x 3' v3", organism = "Homo sapiens", limit = 10)

# PacBio / Oxford Nanopore studies
LongreadSummary()
lf <- LongreadFacets()
lf[lf$facet == "technology", ]
LongreadProjects(technology = "Oxford Nanopore", limit = 10)

# studies submitted from one country (ISO2 code)
CountrySummary("IN")
cf <- CountryFacets("IN")
head(cf[cf$facet == "organism", ])
CountryProjects("IN", organism = "Homo sapiens", limit = 10)
```

The tissue and disease functions take a free-text term. The server finds the
term in UBERON or MONDO and adds its descendants. The values `"rare"` and
`"nord"` select curated disease catalogs:

```{r ontology-collections}
TissueSummary("liver")
tf <- TissueFacets("liver")
head(tf[tf$facet == "organism", ])
TissueProjects("liver", limit = 10)

DiseaseAliases("marfan", limit = 3) # a colloquial name -> its MONDO ids

DiseaseSummary("rare")
df <- DiseaseFacets("rare")
head(df[df$facet == "category", ])
DiseaseProjects("rare", organism = "Homo sapiens", limit = 10) # or a MONDO term
```

## Construct sample cohorts

`SampleSearch()` uses harmonized metadata to find samples in all studies. You must give one or more filters.

```{r cohort}
liver <- SampleSearch(
  organism = "Homo sapiens",
  sex = "female",
  tissue = "liver",
  age_min_years = 50
)

head(liver[, c("sample", "study_accession", "tissue", "disease", "assay", "age")])
```

The `total` attribute holds the number of matches:

```{r cohort-total}
attr(liver, "total")
```

### Cohort search filters

| Filter Group | Arguments |
| --- | --- |
| Harmonized Attributes | `organism`, `tissue`, `disease`, `cell_type`, `assay`, `sex`, `strain`, `treatment`, and other sample metadata fields. |
| Harmonized Ontology IDs | `disease_ontology_id`, `tissue_ontology_id`, `cell_type_ontology_id`, `assay_ontology_id`, `development_stage_ontology_id`. |
| Value Ranges | `age_min_years`, `age_max_years`, `min_cell_count`, `max_cell_count`, `min_gene_count`, `max_gene_count`. |
| Read-Derived Metrics | `single_cell_only`, `has_viral_reads`, `has_bacterial_reads`, `hpv_type`, `microbe`, `microbe_class`, `microbe_min_breadth`, `microbe_min_kmer_mass`, `microbe_validated_only`. |

`age_min_years = 0` keeps all the samples that have a recorded age.

### Query by ontology ID and descendants

An ontology ID also finds the samples that are mapped to its descendant subtypes:

```{r cohort-ontology}
nrow(SampleSearch(disease_ontology_id = "MONDO:0005061", limit = 200))
```

`include_descendants = FALSE` finds only the exact term:

```{r cohort-exact}
nrow(SampleSearch(
  disease_ontology_id = "MONDO:0005061",
  include_descendants = FALSE, limit = 200
))
```

### Filter by read-derived microbial screen

`microbe` keeps the samples that have reads from that microbe. It also adds the detection counts:

```{r cohort-microbes}
hpv <- SampleSearch(
  tissue = "cervix",
  microbe = "HPV",
  sort = "cell_count",
  order = "desc",
  limit = 10
)

hpv[, c("sample", "study_accession", "cells", "hpv_top_type", "microbe_n_detections")]
```

> [!NOTE]
> Use the name of the organism (`"HPV"`). More general terms, for example `"papillomavirus"`, do not match.

### A worked cohort: HPV16 in single-cell cervical cancer

Add one filter at a time. After each filter, read `total` to see how the filter makes the cohort smaller:

```{r cohort-hpv-funnel}
cervical <- SampleSearch(disease_ontology_id = "MONDO:0002974", limit = 1)
attr(cervical, "total")

sc <- SampleSearch(
  disease_ontology_id = "MONDO:0002974",
  single_cell_only = TRUE,
  limit = 1
)
attr(sc, "total")
```

`MONDO:0002974` is cervical cancer. The search includes its subtypes by default. `hpv_type` keeps the samples with reads that the Pentimento screen called as that strain:

```{r cohort-hpv16}
hpv16 <- SampleSearch(
  disease_ontology_id = "MONDO:0002974",
  single_cell_only = TRUE,
  hpv_type = "HPV16"
)

hpv16[, c("sample", "study_accession", "disease", "cells", "hpv_top_type")]
```

`hpv_type` selects one strain. `microbe = "HPV"` includes all strains. It adds the detections to the `microbes` field of each sample:

```{r cohort-hpv-any}
hpv <- SampleSearch(
  disease_ontology_id = "MONDO:0002974",
  single_cell_only = TRUE,
  microbe = "HPV"
)

MicrobeDetections(hpv)
```

An age filter removes all the samples that have no recorded age. Before you use an age filter, do a check of the age coverage:

```{r cohort-age-coverage}
# age_min_years = 0 means "has a recorded age at all"
with_age <- SampleSearch(
  disease_ontology_id = "MONDO:0002974",
  single_cell_only = TRUE,
  age_min_years = 0,
  limit = 1
)
attr(with_age, "total")
```

`age_days` holds the harmonized age. `age` holds the string from the submitter, in the unit of the submitter.

### The distribution of HPV types across cervical cancer

Remove `single_cell_only`. Keep `microbe = "HPV"`. Count the detections. A sample can have more than one strain. Thus, the sum of the counts is more than the number of samples in the cohort:

```{r cohort-hpv-distribution}
hpv_all <- SampleSearch(disease_ontology_id = "MONDO:0002974", microbe = "HPV")
c(samples = nrow(hpv_all), studies = length(unique(hpv_all$study_accession)))

all_types <- sort(table(MicrobeDetections(hpv_all)$organism), decreasing = TRUE)
all_types
```

That table counts all k-mer hits. Some hits are only a few unitigs on a genome that has almost no coverage. `is_viral_evidence` is the gate of the screen:

```{r cohort-hpv-gated}
gated <- MicrobeDetections(hpv_all, validated_only = TRUE)
gated_types <- sort(table(gated$organism), decreasing = TRUE)
gated_types
```

`breadth_frac` and `kmer_mass` are the inputs of the gate. Use them to set custom thresholds.

The plot shows the two counts on one axis. It shows how much of the tail is trace signal:

```{r cohort-hpv-plot, fig.alt = "Bar chart of HPV type detections across cervical cancer samples, all detections against those passing the viral gate", fig.height = 3.2}
dist <- rbind(
  data.frame(as.data.frame(all_types), set = "any detection"),
  data.frame(as.data.frame(gated_types), set = "passes the gate")
)
names(dist)[1:2] <- c("type", "Freq")

ggplot2::ggplot(dist, ggplot2::aes(stats::reorder(type, Freq), Freq, fill = set)) +
  ggplot2::geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  ggplot2::coord_flip() +
  ggplot2::labs(x = NULL, y = "detections", fill = NULL) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal()
```

`hpv_top_type` covers the samples that the Pentimento single-cell pass processed. `microbes` holds the strain detections that are outside that coverage.

The denominator includes only the screened samples that have detections. Thus, you cannot use these counts to estimate HPV prevalence.

`SeqoutGet()` opens the study of a row. `SeqoutListCounts()` reads the matrices of that study.

## Execute SQL queries offline

The search and cohort functions must have the REST API. For custom aggregation, or for offline queries on the full index, use the Parquet backend. Connect to the Parquet backend. Then write SQL:

```{r parquet}
con <- SeqoutConnect("parquet", quiet = TRUE)

Query("
  SELECT dominant_scientific_name AS organism, count(*) AS n
  FROM unified_metadata
  WHERE n_samples >= 10
  GROUP BY organism
  ORDER BY n DESC
  LIMIT 10
", con = con)
```

`Tables()` lists the tables in the dump. `Query()` registers the tables that a
query names when the query runs. `RegisterTables()` registers them before you
run a query. Then dplyr can get access to them through `con$db`:

```{r tables}
head(Tables(con))
con |> RegisterTables("unified_metadata")
dplyr::tbl(con$db, "unified_metadata") |> head(3)
```

Each query reads the remote Parquet again. `CacheTable()` reads one table into
the connection one time, as `<table>_local`. Queries on that name do not use the
network. `ClearCache()` removes those copies:

```{r cache, eval = FALSE}
CacheTable("geo_series", con = con)
Query("SELECT count(*) FROM geo_series_local", con = con)
ClearCache(con)
```

```{r close}
SeqoutClose(con)
```

To download the dump and make local connections, refer to [Downloads](downloads.html).
